# Everybody Wins — what four decades of Spiel des Jahres rewarded
unit: 1 · kind: book · studied: 2026-08-22

## Mechanism
Wallis's frame (from his talks and published excerpts around the 2023
release): the Spiel des Jahres jury optimizes for the FAMILY TABLE — teach in
minutes, finish in an hour, no player elimination, decisions that feel clever
without deep trees. Era by era the award tracks what the mass market could
absorb: 1980s roll-and-move refinements, 1995 Catan's trading revolution,
2000s gateway German school, 2010s co-ops and party deduction.

## Why it works
**Awards reward teachability; survival rewards replay depth — they are not
the same list.** Wallis notes (Ludology interview, 2023) that several winners
are museum pieces within a decade, while losers like Carcassonne expansions
keep selling. The jury is a proxy for first-play accessibility, nothing more.

## Failure modes
Chasing the award profile produces polite, forgettable games: low interaction,
no tension spikes. Winners that survived all carry one sticky mechanism the
box is named after.

## What it teaches Bob
- Optimize teach-time (≤5 min) AND a single nameable mechanism; both, not either.
- First-play accessibility and 10-play depth are separate gates — score both.
- The one-hour ceiling is a hard mass-market constraint; respect it in target_length.

## Sources
James Wallis, Everybody Wins (2023) — publisher excerpts; Ludology podcast
interview (2023); SdJ jury criteria as published at spiel-des-jahres.de.

PURCHASE RECOMMENDATION: the full year-by-year jury rationale tables exceed
what public materials give — worth the book for the failure years alone.
